prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

Table: Checkout UI Strings (language en).
Grid: 5 columns × 7 rows. Row headers: yes (first logical column identifies each row).
Per-column content facts (content px at 15px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "Key" · longest unbreakable word 206px · one-line width 206px
  col 2: header "English" · longest unbreakable word 62px · one-line width 196px
  col 3: header "中文" · longest unbreakable word 18px · one-line width 184px
  col 4: header "日本語" · longest unbreakable word 25px · one-line width 283px
  col 5: header "العربية" · longest unbreakable word 55px · one-line width 187px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 720px (the dashed pink box = the reader's viewport). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 719px.
Fixed: content, font, 15px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

The image shows the table's content with every cell on one line, so you can read everything. Study it first.
1) Understand it: what is the table for, how will people read, scan and compare it, which columns play the same or similar role, which values must stay intact, which text may wrap naturally, and where existing row height could absorb wrapping.
2) Propose 3 genuinely different column-width designs for 720px (different strategies, not small variations).
Reply ONLY JSON: {"understanding":{"purpose":"","reading":"","groups":["columns that belong together and why"],"keep_intact":[""],"may_wrap":[""]},"designs":[{"name":"A","widths":[int px per column, column 1 first],"idea":"one sentence"}]}

log.raw: {"understanding":{"purpose":"Compare checkout interface strings across four languages, using stable keys to identify each message.","reading":"Readers scan the key column to find a message, then read across its row to compare translations. Each row should remain a clear unit even when translations wrap.","groups":["English, 中文, 日本語, and العربية are parallel translations of the same message and should have a comparable visual role.","Key is the row identifier and needs enough width for the longest unbroken identifier."],"keep_intact":["Keys and other unbreakable words","Numeric ranges such as 3–5"],"may_wrap":["Translation phrases at natural word or character boundaries","Shorter translations can remain on one line while longer translations use the row height created by another language."]},"designs":[{"name":"A","widths":[227,125,110,145,117],"idea":"Give Japanese extra room for its longer phrases while keeping the four translation columns reasonably balanced."},{"name":"B","widths":[227,150,100,132,115],"idea":"Favor English readability, using compact Chinese text and natural wrapping in the other translations."},{"name":"C","widths":[227,112,95,160,130],"idea":"Prioritize the longer Japanese and Arabic translations, accepting more wrapping in English and Chinese."}]}
